title: Advertising
objective: After this level you can explain how advertising shapes what people buy.
summary: Advertising can inform (eyeglasses cost more where ads were banned) and persuade (brand loyalty, "A Diamond Is Forever"). Pigou argued rival ads may simply cancel out.

cards.headline: Four words from 1947: "A Diamond Is Forever."
cards.body: Copywriter Frances Gerety wrote them for De Beers. In 1999, Advertising Age named them the best advertising slogan of the 20th century. How can a few words change what people buy?

cards.headline: Ads that inform
cards.body: Some ads are simply news: this exists, here's what it does, here's the price. That helps you compare. In 1972, economist Lee Benham found that eyeglasses cost more in US states that banned advertising than in states that allowed it. When shoppers can't see prices, they can't easily compare them.

cards.headline: Ads that persuade
cards.body: Other ads work on feelings. Blindfolded, many people can't tell common ketchups apart, yet habit and advertising give them strong favorites. De Beers's four words helped make the diamond solitaire the standard engagement ring. Before, engagement rings often used colored gems, small diamonds or even pearls. The stone didn't change. The story around it did.

cards.fact: Rival ads can cancel each other out.
cards.context: In 1920, economist A. C. Pigou pointed out that when two competing firms each spend to lure customers from the other, the spending may simply neutralize itself, leaving both where they'd be if neither had advertised. Picture two neighbors in a shouting match: both get louder, and nobody hears anything new.

cards.headline: Advertising: decoded
learned: Ads can inform: Benham's eyeglass prices
Ads can persuade: habit and brand loyalty
"A Diamond Is Forever" (1947) reshaped engagement rings
Rival ads may cancel out, as Pigou argued

questions.prompt: What did Lee Benham find about eyeglass prices in 1972?

options.label: They were lower where ads were banned
options.rationale: The opposite: they were higher where ads were banned.

options.label: They were the same in every state
options.rationale: Prices differed with the advertising rules.

options.label: They were higher where ads were banned
They rose wherever optometrists advertised
options.rationale: The opposite: prices were higher where ads were banned.

questions.explanation: Eyeglasses cost more in states that banned advertising: ads helped shoppers compare prices.

questions.prompt: Blindfolded, many people can't tell ketchups apart, yet they have strong favorites. What does this show?

options.label: All ketchup brands use one recipe
options.rationale: The point is people can't taste a difference, not that recipes match.

options.label: Blindfolds dull people's sense of taste
options.rationale: The test shows preferences come from habit and ads.

options.label: Ads only work on expensive goods
options.rationale: Ketchup is cheap, and ads still shape preferences.

questions.explanation: When people can't taste a difference but still have favorites, habit and advertising are doing the work.

questions.prompt: Pigou said rival ads can cancel out. From Level 11, profit is what's left after costs. What do such ads do to it?

options.label: Raise it, since ads always win customers
options.rationale: Cancelled-out ads win no one new.

options.label: Shrink it: more cost, no gain
Leave it unchanged, since ads are free
Double it, since both firms advertised
options.rationale: Both firms end up where they started, minus the spend.

questions.explanation: The ads leave each firm where it started, but the spending is a cost, so less is left as profit.
